In a GAN trained using the original minimax (saturating) generator objective, suppose the discriminator becomes nearly perfect very early in training. What will be the most likely consequence of this?
options: The generator learns faster because the discriminator provides perfect classification.
Both the generator and discriminator converge immediately to the optimal solution.
The generator's loss becomes zero, indicating perfect image generation.
The generator stops learning because it receives very small (vanishing) gradients.
questions.correct_answer: The generator stops learning because it receives very small (vanishing) gradients.

Suppose the residual connections in the transformer block are removed, so the forward pass becomes: [IMAGE: /data/images/da2001_2026T2_ET_AN_p6_Im1.webp|block] What is the most likely consequence of this change as more transformer blocks ( [IMAGE: /data/images/da2001_2026T2_ET_AN_p6_Im2.webp|inline] ) are stacked?
options: No meaningful effect - LayerNorm already keeps activations well-scaled, so the residual path is redundant.

Gradients have no direct path back to earlier layers, so as depth increases they must propagate entirely through each sub-layer's transformation, making them prone to vanishing or exploding and the network much harder to optimize.
The model would no longer be able to apply the causal mask correctly, since masking depends on the residual stream.
Training would fail immediately with a shape mismatch error, since the residual connection is required to keep tensor dimensions consistent.

questions.correct_answer: Gradients have no direct path back to earlier layers, so as depth increases they must propagate entirely through each sub-layer's transformation, making them prone to vanishing or exploding and the network much harder to optimize.
